cases.summary: PayPal "account suspended" email from a look-alike address, link text shows paypal.com

input.pageTitle: Your account has been suspended - Gmail
input.visibleText: We noticed unusual activity on your account. Verify your account within 24 hours or it will be closed.

reasons.explanation: A link says it goes to paypal.com, PayPal's real website, but it really goes to paypa1-secure.example.
A link pretends to be PayPal, but it goes to paypa1-secure.example, not PayPal's real website.
This looks like an official notice from PayPal, but it came from alerts@paypa1-secure.example, not one of PayPal's own email addresses.
The sender's address (alerts@paypa1-secure.example) pretends to be PayPal, but it isn't PayPal's real address.
This email says it's from PayPal, but none of its links go to PayPal's real website (one goes to paypa1-secure.example).
It says something is wrong with your account. This is a common trick to get you to log in on a fake page.
It tries to rush you. Real companies give you time to think.

cases.why: Fake sender, look-alike address, a link that says paypal.com but goes elsewhere, and an account threat.

cases.summary: "Microsoft account team" from a free Gmail account about an unusual sign-in

input.visibleText: We detected a sign-in to your account from a new location. Click below to secure your account.

reasons.explanation: The sender's name says Microsoft, but it came from a free personal email account (ms.account.team.alerts@gmail.com). Microsoft never does this.
This email says it's from Microsoft, but none of its links go to Microsoft's real website (one goes to secure-account-review.example).
It says something is wrong with your account. This is a common trick to get you to log in on a fake page.

cases.why: Microsoft never sends account alerts from a free personal email account.

cases.summary: Apple ID sign-in page on a free hosting website

input.pageTitle: Sign in with your Apple ID

reasons.explanation: This page looks like a sign-in or payment page for Apple, but it is on appleid-verify.netlify.app, not Apple's real website.
This website's name pretends to be Apple, but appleid-verify.netlify.app is not Apple's real website.
This page asks for a password or card number, but it's on appleid-verify.netlify.app, a free website anyone can make. Real banks and companies never do this.

cases.why: A company sign-in page on a free website anyone can make, under a look-alike name.
